# U.S. Business Cycle Update

Report 028 | Published 2020-08-02 | Evaluated 2026-11-07

[Original member article](https://www.lynalden.com/premium-2020-8-2/) | [Article index](README.md) | [Structured review](../data/reviews/028.json)

Uneven recovery and an approaching fiscal gap.

The near-term Texas mortality direction and housing rebound were supported. July jobs improved more than the leveling-off language suggests, and PPP timing remains overstated. The homeownership jump needs a material survey-bias caveat. New checks arrived, but the broad fiscal compromise was delayed until December.

**Coverage:** All numbered text blocks and image labels read. Material theses, forecasts and explanations are included; routine holdings lists, incidental statistics, company descriptions and boilerplate are excluded. Chart pixels were not inspected.

## Claims

### 028-C01

**Deaths should flatten after cases**

| Field | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Verdict | Right |
| Type | forecast |
| Horizon | coming weeks |
| Conditions | Not specified |
| Author modality | probably |
| Asset or variable | Texas deaths |
| Source blocks | 11, 15, 16, 17 |
| Thesis family | covid-death-lag |

The Texas seven-day fatalities measure fell from 233.29 at August 2 to 179.43 at August 16 and 108.14 at August 30. This supports the coming-weeks direction for the highlighted state. Later-vintage finalized data differ from daily publication reports and do not verify every national comparison.

**Direction:** Resolved as stated.

**Timing:** Original horizon retained: coming weeks

**Mechanism:** Outcome evidence does not independently identify causation.

**Reviewer confidence:** medium

**Outcome evidence:**

- [Historical Texas dashboard data](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/chs/data/COVID/CaseCountData.xlsx) | Texas DSHS | 2023-05-10 | Verified in the audit

Archived Trends sheet Total Fatalities Current Day: seven-day averages ending July 5, July 19, August 2, August 16, August 30, 2020 were 118.00,242.14,233.29,179.43,108.14. Later-vintage data, not contemporary reporting snapshots.

### 028-C02

**PPP expiry slows jobs recovery**

| Field | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Verdict | Mixed |
| Type | explanation |
| Horizon | Not specified |
| Conditions | Not specified |
| Author modality | asserted |
| Asset or variable | US jobs |
| Source blocks | 22, 23, 24 |
| Thesis family | ppp-expiry-layoffs |

July hiring slowed relative to June, but still added 1.8 m payroll jobs and unemployment declined. PPP forgiveness periods had been extended, so the general end-June maturity claim and causal attribution are too strong.

**Direction:** See reason; no return inferred.

**Timing:** No fixed endpoint supplied.

**Mechanism:** Outcome evidence does not independently identify causation.

**Reviewer confidence:** medium

**Outcome evidence:**

- [July 2020 employment situation](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/empsit_08072020.htm) | BLS | 2020-08-07 | Verified in the audit

Payrolls rose 1.8 m in July after 4.8 m in June and 2.7 m in May; unemployment fell to 10.2%. Permanent job losers were approximately unchanged at 2.9 m in July; temporary layoffs fell 1.3 m.

- [PPP Flexibility Act implementation](https://legacy.sba.gov/article/2020/jun/08/joint-statement-sba-administrator-jovita-carranza-us-treasury-secretary-steven-t-mnuchin-regarding-0) | SBA / Treasury | 2020-06-08 | Verified in the audit

Forgiveness covered period extended to 24 weeks; prior borrowers could elect eight weeks. Loan maturity was distinct, generally two or five years, not end-June 2020.

### 028-C04

**Claims imply thirty million beneficiaries**

| Field | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Verdict | Wrong |
| Type | empirical |
| Horizon | Not specified |
| Conditions | Not specified |
| Author modality | asserted |
| Asset or variable | US benefits |
| Source blocks | 26, 48 |
| Thesis family | ui-claims-persons-confusion |

Claim weeks were not a reliable distinct-person count, as GAO documented. The extra-benefit expiry was real, but multiplying a claim total into the number of affected people needs deduplication and eligibility checks.

**Direction:** See reason; no return inferred.

**Timing:** No fixed endpoint supplied.

**Mechanism:** Business performance and shareholder return are distinct.

**Reviewer confidence:** medium

**Outcome evidence:**

- [COVID-19 oversight report](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-21-265/index.html) | GAO | 2021-01-28 | Verified in the audit

GAO found continued-claim totals counted weeks, not unique beneficiaries. DOL clarified this in December 2020; backlogs could produce several weeks per person in one report.

### 028-C07

**New-home sales rebound rapidly**

| Field | Assessment |
| --- | --- |

| Horizon | Not specified |
| Conditions | Not specified |
| Author modality | asserted |
| Asset or variable | US new homes |
| Source blocks | 34, 37 |

The contemporary June release showed 776,000 annualized sales, above May and year-earlier point estimates, supporting the sector-specific rebound. Confidence intervals were wide; this does not imply the entire economy recovered equally.

**Direction:** Resolved as stated.

**Timing:** No fixed endpoint supplied.

**Mechanism:** Business performance and shareholder return are distinct.

**Reviewer confidence:** medium

**Outcome evidence:**

- [June 2020 new residential sales](https://www.census.gov/construction/nrs/pdf/newressales_202006.pdf) | Census / HUD | 2020-07-24 | Verified in the audit

June new-home sales were 776,000 annualized versus revised May 682,000, a 13.8% point estimate increase with a wide confidence interval; June 2019 estimate was 726,000.

### 028-C08

**Homeownership jumps in one quarter**

| Field | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Verdict | Mixed |
| Type | empirical |
| Horizon | Not specified |
| Conditions | Not specified |
| Author modality | asserted |
| Asset or variable | Homeownership |
| Source blocks | 38 |
| Thesis family | housing-survey-pandemic-bias |

The published estimate rose 2.6 percentage points, not 2.6 percent relative. Later Census research found pandemic nonresponse likely inflated the rate, so the quoted observation is real but interpreting it as entirely actual ownership change is not justified.

**Direction:** See reason; no return inferred.

**Timing:** No fixed endpoint supplied.

**Mechanism:** Business performance and shareholder return are distinct.

**Reviewer confidence:** medium

**Outcome evidence:**

- [Pandemic effects on housing vacancy survey](https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2022/demo/SEHSD-WP2022-11.html) | Census Bureau | 2022-05-17 | Verified in the audit

Nonresponse changes likely elevated Q2/Q3 2020 homeownership estimates; effects dissipated by Q4. The reported jump cannot be interpreted wholly as actual households purchasing homes.

A major compromise eventually became law in December, but much later than this month's focus, and its COVID relief component was below the suggested over-$1 tn floor. Whole appropriations totals should not be substituted for incremental relief. The exact size requires a consistent program-scoring basis.

**Direction:** See reason; no return inferred.

**Timing:** Original horizon retained: next fiscal round

**Mechanism:** Outcome evidence does not independently identify causation.

**Reviewer confidence:** medium

**Outcome evidence:**

- [CARES and Consolidated Appropriations Acts](https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/coronavirus/about-the-cares-act) | US Treasury | Verified in the audit

The subsequent broad relief act passed Congress December 21 and was signed December 27, 2020, after the election rather than during summer.
